Get to know the data before modeling anything. Every chart here should end with one sentence saying what it shows.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

# Run the scripts in R/ first (see the README).
ercot <- read_rds(here::here("data/processed/ercot_hourly.rds"))
```

## Sanity checks
### Check 1: Do the time stamps line up?

Solar output should peak around 1 p.m. Central. A peak at noon or 2 p.m. would
mean the hour conversion is off by one.

```{r}
#| label: check-solar-peak
#| code-summary: "Code: solar output by hour"

ercot |>
  filter(hub == "HB_BUSAVG") |>   # grid data repeats for every hub; use one
  group_by(hour_local) |>
  summarise(avg_solar = mean(solar_mw, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(hour_local, avg_solar)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Hour of day (Central)", y = "Average solar output (MW)",
       title = "Solar output peaks in the 1 p.m. hour")
```

**Findings:** Solar output peaks in the 1–2 p.m. Central hour, as expected for
Texas, so the generation data and prices are aligned hour for hour.

### Check 2: Missing data

How many hours are missing for each source, and are they clustered or scattered?

```{r}
#| label: check-missing-counts
#| code-summary: "Code: missing hours by column"

ercot |>
  filter(hub == "HB_BUSAVG") |>
  summarise(across(c(rt_price, da_price, demand_mw, wind_mw, solar_mw, gas_mw),
                   ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Missing hours, 2021–2025")
```

```{r}
#| label: check-missing-months
#| code-summary: "Code: missing hours by month"

ercot |>
  filter(hub == "HB_BUSAVG") |>
  mutate(any_missing = if_any(c(demand_mw, wind_mw, solar_mw, gas_mw), is.na)) |>
  count(year, month, wt = any_missing, name = "missing_hours") |>
  filter(missing_hours > 0) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Months with missing grid data")
```

**Findings:** No prices are missing. Demand is missing for 1 hour and generation
for X hours; these are isolated gaps and are dropped.

### Check 3: Are yearly prices plausible?

```{r}
#| label: check-yearly-prices
#| code-summary: "Code: average price by year"

ercot |>
  group_by(year, hub) |>
  summarise(avg_rt = mean(rt_price), avg_da = mean(da_price), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = hub, values_from = c(avg_rt, avg_da)) |>
  select(year, avg_rt_HB_BUSAVG, avg_da_HB_BUSAVG, avg_rt_HB_WEST, avg_rt_HB_HOUSTON) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Average price by year ($/MWh)")
```

**Findings:** Bus-average real-time prices fell from \$149/MWh in 2021 (Winter
Storm Uri) to \$27 in 2024, then rose to \$32 in 2025, following natural gas
prices. The 2023–2024 averages match Modo Energy's published figures within \$1.

## The grid over time

### How have wind and solar grown?

```{r}
#| label: grid-growth-chart
#| code-summary: "Code: average generation by fuel and year"

grid <- ercot |> filter(hub == "HB_BUSAVG")   # grid data repeats for every hub

grid |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(across(c(gas_mw, wind_mw, solar_mw, coal_mw, nuclear_mw, storage_mw),
                   ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "fuel", values_to = "avg_mw") |>
  mutate(fuel = str_remove(fuel, "_mw") |> str_to_title()) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, avg_mw, colour = fuel)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average output (MW)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Average ERCOT generation by fuel, 2021–2025")
```

```{r}
#| label: grid-growth-table
#| code-summary: "Code: wind and solar share of demand by year"

grid |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    wind_mw     = mean(wind_mw, na.rm = TRUE),
    solar_mw    = mean(solar_mw, na.rm = TRUE),
    demand_mw   = mean(demand_mw, na.rm = TRUE),
    wind_share  = wind_mw / demand_mw,
    solar_share = solar_mw / demand_mw
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 3, 3),
               caption = "Average output (MW) and share of demand")
```

**Findings:** Solar grew fast, more than four times larger from 2021 to 2025.
By 2025 it produced more power than nuclear or coal. Wind grew a little (about
20%). Gas is still the biggest source. Battery data only starts in late 2024,
so storage is shown for 2025 only.

### What does an average day look like?

Summer is June–August and winter is December–February. Price uses the
**median**, so a few extreme hours (like Winter Storm Uri) don't distort the
daily shape.

```{r}
#| label: grid-daily-profile
#| code-summary: "Code: average day by season"
#| fig-height: 7

daily <- grid |>
  mutate(season = case_when(
    month(time_local) %in% 6:8       ~ "Summer",
    month(time_local) %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "Winter"
  )) |>
  filter(!is.na(season)) |>
  group_by(season, hour_local) |>
  summarise(
    `Demand (MW)`       = mean(demand_mw, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Wind (MW)`         = mean(wind_mw, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Solar (MW)`        = mean(solar_mw, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Net load (MW)`     = mean(net_load_mw, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Median RT price ($/MWh)` = median(rt_price),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

daily |>
  pivot_longer(-c(season, hour_local), names_to = "measure") |>
  ggplot(aes(hour_local, value, colour = season)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Hour of day (Central)", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       title = "An average day on the ERCOT grid, summer vs. winter")
```

```{r}
#| label: grid-daily-peaks
#| code-summary: "Code: peak hours by season"

daily |>
  group_by(season) |>
  summarise(
    demand_peak_hour = hour_local[which.max(`Demand (MW)`)],
    net_load_peak_hour = hour_local[which.max(`Net load (MW)`)],
    price_peak_hour  = hour_local[which.max(`Median RT price ($/MWh)`)],
    price_low_hour   = hour_local[which.min(`Median RT price ($/MWh)`)]
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Hour of day when each measure peaks (Central)")
```

**Findings:** Power is most expensive in the evening, not when demand is
highest. In summer, demand peaks around 4–5 p.m., but prices peak around
7–8 p.m., as solar power drops off in the early evening. In winter, prices are lowest in
the afternoon, when solar is strongest. Wind does the opposite of solar: it
blows hardest at night.

## Prices

### How are hourly prices distributed?

Most hours are cheap, but a few are extremely expensive. A **pseudo-log** scale
spreads out the cheap hours while still fitting the \$9,000 spikes and
negative prices on one chart.

```{r}
#| label: prices-distribution
#| code-summary: "Code: distribution of hourly prices"

ercot |>
  filter(hub == "HB_BUSAVG") |>
  ggplot(aes(rt_price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 80) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = scales::pseudo_log_trans(sigma = 10),
                     breaks = c(-100, -10, 0, 10, 25, 50, 100, 1000, 9000)) +
  labs(x = "Real-time price (\\$/MWh, pseudo-log scale)", y = "Hours",
       title = "Hourly real-time prices at the bus-average hub, 2021–2025")
```

```{r}
#| label: prices-extremes
#| code-summary: "Code: negative and extreme price hours by year"

ercot |>
  filter(hub == "HB_BUSAVG") |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    median_price   = median(rt_price),
    mean_price     = mean(rt_price),
    negative_hours = sum(rt_price < 0),
    hours_over_1000 = sum(rt_price > 1000)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Real-time prices by year (bus-average hub)")
```

**Findings:** Most hours are cheap, around \$20–30/MWh. A small number of very
expensive hours pull the average up to more than twice the median. The highest
prices, about \$9,000/MWh, all came during Winter Storm Uri in February 2021,
when regulators held prices at the cap; the cap was lowered to \$5,000 in 2022.
Prices occasionally go below zero, when wind and solar produce more power than
the grid needs.

### How do the hubs differ?

```{r}
#| label: prices-hubs-table
#| code-summary: "Code: price statistics by hub"

ercot |>
  group_by(hub) |>
  summarise(
    median_price  = median(rt_price),
    mean_price    = mean(rt_price),
    p95_price     = quantile(rt_price, 0.95),
    pct_negative  = mean(rt_price < 0) * 100
  ) |>
  arrange(median_price) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Real-time prices by hub, 2021–2025")
```

```{r}
#| label: prices-west-vs-wind
#| code-summary: "Code: West hub discount vs. wind output"

west_vs_wind <- ercot |>
  filter(hub %in% c("HB_WEST", "HB_BUSAVG")) |>
  select(hour_start_utc, hub, rt_price, wind_mw) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = hub, values_from = rt_price) |>
  mutate(wind_bin = cut(wind_mw, breaks = seq(0, 30000, 5000),
                        labels = c("0–5k", "5–10k", "10–15k", "15–20k", "20–25k", "25–30k"))) |>
  filter(!is.na(wind_bin)) |>
  group_by(wind_bin) |>
  summarise(west_minus_system = median(HB_WEST - HB_BUSAVG), hours = n())

ggplot(west_vs_wind, aes(wind_bin, west_minus_system)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("$%.2f", west_minus_system)),
            vjust = ifelse(west_vs_wind$west_minus_system < 0, 1.5, -0.5)) +
  geom_text(aes(y = 1.5, label = paste(scales::comma(hours), "hours")),
            size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(min(west_vs_wind$west_minus_system) - 1.5, 2.5)) +
  labs(x = "ERCOT wind output (MW)",
       y = "West price minus statewide price ($/MWh, median)",
       title = "West Texas power gets cheaper only on very windy hours",
       subtitle = "Below 20,000 MW of wind, West and the rest of Texas pay about the same")
```

**Findings:** The West hub is priced the same as the rest of Texas until wind
output passes about 20,000 MW. Above that, West is about \$6/MWh cheaper, and
about \$10 cheaper above 25,000 MW. Most Texas wind farms are in West Texas,
and on very windy hours the power lines carrying that power east fill up, so
the extra power is stuck in the West and its price drops.
